title: Multi-token prediction: training GPTs to look ahead
summary: Train a GPT to predict several future tokens per position: parallel heads, DeepSeek-V3's sequential modules, both built in your own GPT, the wider design space, and reusing MTP to decode faster.
outcomes: Explain how the multi-token loss adds n targets per position without changing the input or context
Compute the loss and peak logit memory of an n-head model and the memory saved by per-head backward passes
Explain the choice-point and mutual-information arguments and when MTP helps or hurts
Trace DeepSeek-V3's sequential MTP module: its inputs, index alignment and weighted loss
Implement both MTP designs in a GPT with correct target shifts, and test them against the next-token loss
Compare ProphetNet, parallel heads, sequential modules and registers, and explain why retrofitting heads works poorly
Compute expected tokens per forward pass for self-speculative decoding from per-position acceptance rates

lessons.title: From one target per position to n targets per position

blocks.md: In the GPT you built, every position $t$ of a training sequence produces one prediction: a distribution over the vocabulary for the **next** token $x_{t+1}$. The loss is the average cross-entropy of those predictions, and teacher forcing feeds the true prefix at every position. This is next-token prediction, and it is the objective behind GPT and Meta's Llama family of open models.

Gloeckle et al. (FAIR, Meta's Fundamental AI Research lab, 2024) argue that this objective is an inefficient teacher. Each position is graded only on what comes immediately next, so the model can drive the loss down by latching on to **local** patterns. Decisions whose consequences show up several tokens later (which function to call, which branch of an argument to take) get no more weight than a choice between synonyms.

**Multi-token prediction (MTP)** changes the question asked at each position. Instead of only the next token, the model predicts the next $n$ tokens $x_{t+1}, \dots, x_{t+n}$, each from the same context $x_{1:t}$. Each prediction comes from its own output **head**: a small final layer that reads the model's internal vector at position $t$ and turns it into a distribution over the vocabulary, so head $i$ predicts the token $i$ steps ahead. The extra predictions are an **auxiliary task**: a second training signal added to the main one, used to shape the shared representation (the internal vectors that every head reads). Let us see what that does to the training targets on a tiny sequence.

blocks.title: Targets per position: n = 1 versus n = 3

scenes.caption: An 8-token training sequence. Row labels name what each prediction head would be asked for; nothing is predicted yet.
Next-token prediction: position t is graded on token t+1. Seven positions have a target, so the sequence contributes 7 loss terms.
Add a second head for token t+2. Position 3 ('sat') must now also predict 'the'. Six more targets: 13 loss terms from the same 8 tokens.
With n = 3, each position answers three questions from one context. Head i has 8 - i targets, so 7 + 6 + 5 = 18 loss terms. Same data, denser supervision.

Read one column: at position 3 the model sees only 'the cat sat' and must commit to 'on', 'the', 'mat'. It cannot see the tokens it predicts, so the representation at t must carry information about where the text is going.

blocks.caption: The multi-token loss of Gloeckle et al. In words: for every position t and every offset i from 1 to n, add minus the log-probability that the model, with weights theta, gives the true token i steps ahead. Each term is one cross-entropy; with n = 1 it is the ordinary next-token loss.

blocks.md: Two clarifications prevent most confusion. First, the $n$ predictions at position $t$ are made **in parallel** from the same context; head 2 never sees head 1's guess. That is why the loss is a plain sum of separate log-probabilities, not a joint probability of the $n$-token block. Second, this changes training only. At inference time the simplest use is to keep just the next-token head and decode exactly like any GPT.

Common misconception: an MTP model does not have to emit several tokens per step. Gloeckle et al. use only the next-token head for ordinary decoding. The other heads are optional, and lesson 7 shows how they can be reused to draft tokens for faster decoding.

blocks.prompt: If MTP adds more loss terms per sequence, does it also increase the number of tokens the model is trained on?
blocks.reveal: No. The training corpus and the number of forward passes over it are unchanged. MTP extracts **more targets from each position** of the same data. The report on DeepSeek-V3 (a large open model from the lab DeepSeek, covered in lesson 4) puts it as 'densifies the training signals'. Whether denser signals actually help is an empirical question, which lesson 3 answers with numbers.

blocks.md: Multi-token prediction keeps the input and the causal context the same and only adds targets: each position is asked for tokens t+1 through t+n, all from the prefix ending at t.

blocks.question: A 10-token sequence is trained with n = 4 independent future heads. How many loss terms does it contribute (count head i as having 10 - i targets)?
options: 9, because only the next-token head counts
40, because each of 10 positions has 4 targets
36, because 4 x 9
blocks.explain: Head 1 has targets for positions 1 to 9, head 2 for positions 1 to 8, and so on: 9 + 8 + 7 + 6 = 30. Positions near the end have fewer valid future tokens, so the count is not simply 10 x 4.

blocks.question: During training, what does the head that predicts x(t+3) receive as input at position t?
options: The shared representation of the prefix x(1..t) only
The prefix plus head 1's and head 2's predicted tokens
The true tokens x(t+1) and x(t+2), via teacher forcing
The whole sequence, with future tokens masked out after the loss
blocks.explain: In the Gloeckle design all heads read the same shared representation of the prefix ending at t and predict in parallel. No head sees other heads' guesses or any token after t. (DeepSeek-V3 makes a different choice, covered in lesson 4.)

lessons.title: Shared trunk, n heads, and the memory trick that keeps it cheap

blocks.md: Gloeckle et al. split the transformer into three parts. A **shared trunk** $f_s$ (most of the layers) turns the context $x_{1:t}$ into a hidden state $z_t$: the vector of size $d$ (the model's hidden size) that the last trunk layer outputs at position $t$. There are $n$ **independent heads** $f_{h_i}$, each a single transformer layer. Finally one **shared unembedding** $f_u$ maps a head's output to vocabulary logits. The unembedding is the final linear layer you built as `lm_head`, a $d \times V$ matrix; it is named for undoing the embedding, turning a vector back into one score per vocabulary token.

blocks.caption: In words: head i's distribution is the softmax of the unembedding applied to head i applied to the trunk output. Head 1 is the next-token head. Every head reads the same trunk output and uses the same unembedding matrix.

blocks.title: Gloeckle et al. architecture with n = 4 heads

scenes.caption: Start from a plain GPT: context in, trunk, one output layer, a next-token distribution.
Add three more heads on the same trunk output z_t. Each head is one transformer layer, so heads can specialize to their offset.
All heads share one unembedding matrix (size d x V), so the expensive vocabulary projection is not copied n times.
Compute-matched comparison: when n - 1 head layers are added, n - 1 layers are removed from the trunk, so the MTP model has the same parameter count as its baseline.
At inference, the default is to run trunk and head 1 only, which is an ordinary next-token model. Heads 2 to 4 are dimmed: optional extras.

blocks.md: A tiny worked example shows what one position contributes to the loss. Take a 5-token vocabulary {sat, on, the, mat, cat}, context 'the cat', and $n = 3$, so the targets are 'sat', 'on', 'the'. Each head produces its own logits; the shared unembedding is already folded into them here.

blocks.title: One position, three heads: softmax and loss

scenes.caption: Head 1, logits [2.0, 0.5, 0.1, -1.0, 0.3]. Softmax gives p(sat) = 0.623, so the loss term is -ln 0.623 = 0.473.
Head 2 (two steps ahead), logits [0.2, 1.5, 0.4, -0.5, 0.0]. p(on) = 0.509, loss 0.676. Less confident, as expected further out.
Head 3, logits [0.1, 0.3, 1.0, 0.6, 0.2]. p(the) = 0.331, loss 1.106. This position contributes 0.473 + 0.676 + 1.106 = 2.255 to the summed loss.

blocks.md: The cost problem is the unembedding. Vocabulary size $V$ (32k in their token-level runs) is far larger than the hidden size $d$, so the logits tensor and its gradient dominate memory. A naive implementation materializes logits and gradients for all $n$ heads at once, peak memory $O(nV + d)$ per token (each head keeps $V$ logits and $V$ gradient entries, plus the $d$-sized trunk output), which shrinks the batch size you can fit.

Their fix reorders the computation. Run the trunk forward once. Then for each head in turn: forward the head, compute its loss, backward through the head, and **add** the gradient into a buffer at the trunk output, then free that head's logits. Only the $d$-dimensional trunk gradient lives across heads. After the last head, run one backward through the trunk. Peak memory drops to $O(V + d)$.

blocks.title: Forward and backward order for n = 2 heads

scenes.caption: Step 1: one forward pass through the shared trunk produces z for every position.
Head 1 runs forward, computes its loss and immediately backpropagates to the trunk output. Its V-sized logits exist only during this window.
Head 1's logits are freed before head 2 starts. Head 2's gradient is added into the same d-sized buffer at the trunk output.
Finally one backward pass through the trunk with the accumulated gradient. At no moment are two heads' logits alive together, so peak memory is that of one head.

blocks.code:
z = trunk(x)                      # [B, T, d], forward once
z_leaf = z.detach().requires_grad_()
for i, head in enumerate(heads, start=1):
    logits = unembed(head(z_leaf))   # [B, T, V], only one head alive
    loss_i = F.cross_entropy(
        logits[:, :-i].flatten(0, 1),
        x[:, i:].flatten())
    loss_i.backward()                # grads add up in z_leaf.grad
    del logits                       # free V-sized tensors now
z.backward(z_leaf.grad)              # one backward through the trunk
blocks.caption: Sketch of the sequential order in PyTorch style (not the authors' code). Detaching z lets each head backpropagate only to the trunk output, where gradients accumulate.

blocks.md: How big is the saving? A simplified estimate: a micro-batch of 8 sequences x 4096 tokens with $V$ = 32,000, logits and their gradients in bf16 (2 bytes each). A micro-batch is the slice of the batch that one GPU processes in a single forward and backward pass. The format bf16 (bfloat16, the "brain floating point" format from Google Brain) is a 16-bit float that keeps the 8-bit exponent of fp32, the standard 4-byte float, but only 7 mantissa bits, so it covers the same range with less precision. One head's logits are 8 x 4,096 x 32,000 = 1.05 billion values, times 2 bytes = 2.10 GB, and its gradient another 2.10 GB, 4.19 GB together. Holding all heads at once would need 8.39 GB for $n = 2$ and 16.78 GB for $n = 4$; the sequential order needs 4.19 GB for any $n$. (Real frameworks often upcast logits to fp32, which doubles these numbers.)

Training at this scale spreads the model over many GPUs. With FSDP (fully sharded data parallel), each GPU stores only a slice of every layer's weights and gathers the full layer from the others just before using it, running that communication at the same time as computation so it costs little extra time.

Measured cost: relative to next-token training, the paper's Table S5 lists training time of 1.02 to 1.07 for n = 2 and 1.07 to 1.22 for n = 4 across 0.3B to 13B models. The authors attribute this overhead to losing FSDP's overlap of weight communication and compute during the separate per-head backward passes, and say a better implementation can remove it. The next paragraph shows why the split costs overlap.

Why would splitting the backward pass lose that overlap? The PyTorch FSDP paper (Zhao et al., 2023) describes the machinery. Inside one backward pass FSDP **prefetches**: while layer $\ell$ computes its gradients, it already issues the gather of the weights of the layer that runs next, and it sends each finished gradient off to be summed across GPUs (a reduce-scatter) in the background. At the very end of a backward pass, a hook makes FSDP **wait** for all of that pending communication. The per-head schedule calls backward $n + 1$ times per step (once per head, then once for the trunk), and each head's pass covers just one layer plus the shared unembedding. So the closing wait happens $n + 1$ times, and each short pass starts by gathering its head's weights with no earlier layer's compute to hide behind. The paper gives only the one-sentence cause; this mechanism is our reading of how FSDP schedules communication.

blocks.question: A colleague implements MTP with n = 4 by summing four head losses and calling backward once. Training now runs out of memory at the old batch size. What is the most likely cause?
options: The trunk activations are stored four times
All four heads' V-sized logits and gradients are alive at once, so peak memory grows with n
The shared unembedding matrix is copied four times
Cross-entropy needs fp64 when several losses are summed
blocks.explain: Summing losses and calling backward once keeps every head's logits in the graph until the end, so logit memory scales as nV per token. Running forward and backward per head and accumulating the d-sized gradient at the trunk keeps only one head's logits alive.

blocks.question: In the paper's comparisons, a 4-token model and its next-token baseline have equal parameter counts. How?
options: The 4-token model uses a smaller vocabulary
The heads are linear layers with no parameters worth counting
Three layers are removed from the trunk to pay for the three extra head layers
The baseline is trained on four times fewer tokens
blocks.explain: Each head is one transformer layer. Adding n - 1 extra head layers and removing n - 1 trunk layers keeps the total equal, so gains cannot be explained by extra parameters.

lessons.title: Why lookahead helps, and where it does not

blocks.md: Why would extra targets make the next-token head better? The paper offers two arguments, which the authors label as speculation, plus a body of experiments. Start with the arguments, because they also predict where MTP should help most.

**Choice points.** Most tokens in code or prose are easy given the prefix, but a few are **choice points**: decisions that change what follows (which loop to write, what the answer is). Under teacher forcing, a next-token model is graded on a choice point once. With $n$-token prediction, the positions just before the choice point are also asked to predict the choice and its consequences, so the decision shows up in many more loss terms.

blocks.title: Counting loss terms that touch a choice point (n = 3)

scenes.caption: A sequence where every transition is easy except 5 to A, the choice point (after the paper's Figure 9). Tokens after A follow from A.
Next-token prediction grades the choice once: position 5 predicting A.
With n = 3, position 5 must also predict B and C, which depend on the choice of A: 3 terms from position 5.
Position 4 predicts 5, A, B: two terms depend on the choice. Position 3 predicts 4, 5, A: one term. Total 3 + 2 + 1 = 6 = n(n+1)/2.
An easy transition such as 2 to 3 is predicted once per head, n = 3 times. So the choice point gets 6 / 3 = 2 = (n+1)/2 times more relative weight than under next-token training.

blocks.caption: From Appendix L.3, a simplified model of teacher-forced training on optimal trajectories. The n positions up to the choice point touch it in n, n - 1, down to 1 targets, which sum to n(n+1)/2; an easy step is predicted once per head, n terms. Dividing gives (n+1)/2; for n = 4, 10 / 4 = 2.5.

blocks.md: **Mutual information.** Let $X$ be the next token and $Y$ the one after, both given the context. Three quantities from information theory, measured in bits, describe how uncertain they are. The **entropy** $H(X)$ is the average surprise of $X$: the expected value of $-\log_2 p(x)$ over its outcomes. It is also the lowest average cross-entropy any model can reach on $X$, achieved by predicting its true distribution. The **conditional entropy** $H(X \mid Y)$ is the uncertainty about $X$ that is left once $Y$ is known. The **mutual information** $I(X;Y) = H(X) - H(X \mid Y)$ is how much knowing one token tells you about the other; it is symmetric, so it also equals $H(Y) - H(Y \mid X)$. Next-token training at this position targets the entropy $H(X)$; 2-token training targets $H(X) + H(Y)$. Rewriting each entropy with the definition of $I$ and adding the two gives:

blocks.tex: H(X) = H(X \mid Y) + I(X;Y), \qquad H(X) + H(Y) = H(X \mid Y) + 2\,I(X;Y) + H(Y \mid X)
blocks.caption: H(X) + H(Y) is H(X | Y) + 2 I(X;Y) + H(Y | X). The H(Y | X) term is not new: one step later, at position t+1, the next-token head has X in its context and is trained on Y, which is exactly H(Y | X). What the second head adds is a second copy of I(X;Y).

blocks.md: A worked example, computed exactly. Suppose the next token is 'def' or 'class' with probability 0.5 each, and the token after depends on it: p(def, foo) = 0.4, p(def, bar) = 0.1, p(class, Foo) = 0.45, p(class, bar) = 0.05. Summing the joint probabilities gives the distribution of $Y$: foo 0.4, bar 0.1 + 0.05 = 0.15, Foo 0.45. The pair's entropy $H(X,Y)$ applies the same formula to the four joint probabilities, and $I(X;Y) = H(X) + H(Y) - H(X,Y)$. Then $H(X)$ = 1.000 bit, $H(Y)$ = 1.458, $H(X,Y)$ = 1.595, so $I(X;Y)$ = 0.862, $H(X \mid Y)$ = 0.138 and $H(Y \mid X)$ = 0.595. Check: 0.138 + 2(0.862) + 0.595 = 2.458 = $H(X) + H(Y)$. Most of what is uncertain about $X$ is information that is *relevant to what comes next*, and the 2-token loss doubles exactly that part.
These are intuitions, not proofs. The paper itself titles this section 'Why does it work? Some speculation'. Treat them as reasons MTP could help, then check the experiments.

The code results are scored on standard benchmarks. **HumanEval** (OpenAI, 2021) has 164 hand-written Python problems, each a function signature and docstring checked by unit tests. **MBPP** (Mostly Basic Python Problems, Google, 2021) has 974 short entry-level Python tasks. **APPS** has 10,000 problems collected from coding websites, split into introductory, interview and competition levels; APPS/Intro is the introductory part. **pass@k** is the fraction of problems for which at least one of $k$ sampled programs passes all the tests, so pass@1 asks for a correct first try.

**What the experiments show** (models trained on code from scratch, compute-matched):

- Benefits grow with scale. Across six sizes from 0.3B to 13B, MTP is worse than the baseline for small models and better at large ones (at 0.3B and 0.6B the 4-token model is below the baseline on every MBPP and HumanEval score in Table S7). The 13B model solves 12% more HumanEval and 17% more MBPP problems than the next-token model (relative gains).
- The best $n$ depends on data. At 7B on 200B tokens of code with a 32k vocabulary, $n = 4$ won on MBPP and HumanEval; $n = 6$ led on APPS/Intro. For byte-level models, whose tokens are single bytes (a vocabulary of 256) rather than subword pieces, $n = 8$ was best.
- Natural language is mixed. At 7B on 200B tokens, $n = 2$ matched the baseline on six multiple-choice benchmarks and $n = 4$ regressed slightly, while both improved summarization ROUGE-L, a score of how much a generated summary overlaps a reference summary, measured by their longest common subsequence of words.

blocks.title: Choosing n: 7B code models, 200B tokens (Table 1)

scenes.caption: MBPP pass@1. n = 4 reaches 33.8 versus 30.0 for the next-token baseline, +3.8 points. Going further to 6 or 8 gives some of it back.
HumanEval pass@1. n = 4 is again best (24.0 versus 22.8), but n = 6 and n = 8 fall below the baseline. More lookahead is not automatically better.
APPS/Intro pass@100 tells a different story: n = 6 leads with 22.7 versus 17.4. The paper concludes the optimal window likely depends on the data distribution.

blocks.prompt: The induction experiment (induction is copying a pattern seen earlier in the context) trains tiny models (1M to 1B non-embedding parameters, which means not counting the token embedding table) on children's stories with n = 1 and n = 2. Which way do you expect the gap to go as models get larger?
blocks.reveal: 2-token prediction **vastly** improved induction for models of 30M non-embedding parameters and below, but the advantage **disappeared** around 100M. The authors read this as MTP helping a capability form; once it has formed, the task becomes a local next-token problem. This echoes the bigger picture with a twist: on the hardest generative benchmarks, gains appear only at larger scale.

blocks.md:
**Does the advantage survive fine-tuning?** Fine-tuning means continuing to train a pretrained model on a smaller, task-specific dataset. Gloeckle et al. fine-tuned their 7B code models on CodeContests (competitive programming problems, Li et al., 2022), using either the 4-token loss again ($n' = 4$) or plain next-token loss on the MTP model with its extra heads removed ($n' = 1$). Both beat a next-token model fine-tuned the same way, across pass@k for k from 1 to 1000, and $n' = 1$ on top of 4-token pretraining was best overall. The paper only plots these curves (Figure 4), so no exact numbers are quoted here.

The opposite direction did not work. Taking an already trained next-token model, Llama 2, and continuing its training with a 4-token loss on 200B tokens of code gave no significant gain (Table S6). The authors suppose the new loss changes the initialization too brutally for the model to recover.

blocks.title: Adding a 4-token loss to trained Llama 2 (Table S6, code)

scenes.caption: MBPP pass@1 after 200B tokens of code. Next-token training gives 39.6. Linear heads 39.3 and one-layer heads 38.3 do slightly worse; only one-layer heads plus 3 added layers reach 42.5.
HumanEval pass@1: 31.4 for next-token training, and every 4-token variant is lower (29.0, 27.9, 28.7). Pretraining with the MTP loss from the start is what paid off in this paper.

blocks.md: MTP reweights training toward decisions that matter for the continuation. It helps most on generative tasks such as code, at larger model sizes, with n tuned to the data; it is not a free win on every benchmark.

blocks.question: With n = 6, how much more relative weight does a choice point get than an inconsequential transition, under the paper's simplified counting?
options: 6 times
21 times
3.5 times
1 time, since all tokens are weighted equally by cross-entropy
blocks.explain: A choice point is touched by 1 + 2 + ... + 6 = 21 loss terms, an inconsequential step by 6. Relative to next-token training the ratio is 21 / 6 = 3.5 = (n+1)/2.

blocks.question: A team training a 300M-parameter code model switches to 4-token prediction because 'the paper showed +12% on HumanEval'. What is the main risk?
options: None: MTP helps at every scale
Small models were worse than the baseline in the paper; the gains appeared at larger sizes
4-token prediction makes inference 4x slower
HumanEval cannot be evaluated with MTP models
blocks.explain: The scaling sweep showed MTP underperforming next-token training for small models and outperforming it at scale. The 12% figure is for the 13B model. Inference cost is unchanged when only the next-token head is used.

blocks.question: You have a 7B code model pretrained with 4-token prediction and want the best model for a new coding task. Based on Gloeckle et al.'s CodeContests fine-tuning, what should you try first?
options: Fine-tune with the 4-token loss, since the heads are already trained
Fine-tune a next-token-pretrained model with a 4-token loss instead
Skip fine-tuning; MTP models cannot be fine-tuned
Fine-tune with plain next-token loss after dropping the extra heads
blocks.explain: Both ways of fine-tuning the 4-token model beat the next-token baseline, and next-token fine-tuning on top of 4-token pretraining was best overall. Adding a 4-token loss to an already trained next-token model (Llama 2, Table S6) gave no significant gain.

lessons.title: DeepSeek-V3: sequential MTP modules with a full causal chain

blocks.md: DeepSeek-V3 (a 671B-parameter mixture-of-experts model, 37B active per token) adopted MTP, citing Gloeckle et al., but changed the design. In a mixture-of-experts (MoE) model, most feed-forward layers are split into many smaller feed-forward networks called experts, and a small router sends each token to only a few of them, so only 37B of the 671B weights do work for any one token. Gloeckle's heads predict in parallel and independently. DeepSeek-V3 predicts $D$ additional tokens **sequentially** with $D$ small modules, one per extra token, and keeps the **complete causal chain** at each prediction depth (depth $k$ is the $k$-th extra module, which predicts the token $k + 1$ steps ahead): the module predicting two tokens ahead also gets to see the token one ahead.

The $k$-th MTP module has four parts: the **shared** embedding layer, the **shared** output head (both reused from the main model), one transformer block $\mathrm{TRM}_k$, and a projection matrix $M_k$ of shape $d \times 2d$. RMSNorm (root mean square normalization), used in DeepSeek-V3 and Llama, is a simpler cousin of LayerNorm: it divides a vector by the root mean square of its entries, without subtracting the mean, then multiplies by a learned scale. For input position $i$ at depth $k$ the module combines two vectors: the hidden state $h_i^{k-1}$ from the previous depth (the main model's final hidden state when $k = 1$), and the embedding of the token $t_{i+k}$.

blocks.caption: Equations 21 to 23 of the DeepSeek-V3 report. In words: RMSNorm both inputs, concatenate them ([a; b]), project 2d back to d with M_k, run block TRM_k over positions 1 to T - k (T is the sequence length), and apply the shared output head to predict token i + k + 1.

blocks.title: Main model plus one MTP module (D = 1)

scenes.caption: The main model is an ordinary next-token model: embed, 61 transformer layers, output head, loss on t(i+1).
The MTP module takes the main model's final hidden state h_i and normalizes it.
It also embeds the true next token t(i+1) with the shared embedding. This is the causal chain: the depth-1 prediction is conditioned on the token one step ahead.
The two d-vectors are concatenated and projected back to d by M_1, then pass through one extra transformer block TRM_1 (causal attention over the sequence).
The shared output head turns the result into a distribution for t(i+2). Embedding and head are physically shared with the main model, so the module adds only M_1, the block and its norms.

blocks.title: Index alignment for depth 1 on a 7-token sequence

scenes.caption: A 7-token training sequence.
The main model at position i predicts t(i+1): six targets, t2 to t7.
The depth-1 module at position i embeds the true token t(i+1) (teacher forcing) next to the main model's h_i.

And predicts t(i+2): five targets, t3 to t7. Positions 6 and 7 have no token two ahead. In the report's notation these are T = 6 inputs plus a final target t(T+1), so the module runs on T - k = 5 positions.

blocks.md: The training objective adds the MTP losses to the main loss. Each depth $k$ has an ordinary cross-entropy $\mathcal{L}^k_{\text{MTP}}$ over its targets; these are averaged over the $D$ depths and scaled by a weight $\lambda$ that sets how much the extra losses count relative to the main loss:

blocks.caption: Equation 25. In words: average the D depth losses, scale by lambda, and add the result to the main next-token loss. DeepSeek-V3 uses D = 1, with lambda = 0.3 for the first 10 trillion training tokens and 0.1 for the remaining 4.8 trillion.

blocks.md: Concrete numbers from the released model: `num_nextn_predict_layers` is 1 in `config.json`, and the module is stored as layer 61, right after the main model's layers 0 to 60. The weights documentation lists 11.5B unique module parameters, excluding the shared embedding and output head (about 0.9B each: vocabulary size 129,280 times hidden size 7,168 = 0.93B). At inference the module can be dropped entirely, leaving the main model unchanged. The report's ablation, shown next, scores models on HumanEval and MBPP from lesson 3 plus GSM8K (about 8,500 grade-school math word problems), MATH (12,500 competition mathematics problems) and MMLU (Massive Multitask Language Understanding: multiple-choice questions across 57 subjects).

Why is 'one extra block' 11.5B parameters, more than many whole models? Because it is a DeepSeek-V3 **MoE** block. Counting from `config.json` (hidden size 7,168; 256 routed experts plus 1 shared expert, each a feed-forward network with three 7,168 x 2,048 matrices; DeepSeek's multi-head latent attention (MLA, which compresses keys and values into a small shared latent vector) with 128 heads): the routed experts hold 256 x 3 x 7,168 x 2,048 = 11.27B, attention 0.19B, the shared expert 0.04B and the router 0.002B, so the block is 11.51B. The projection $M_1$ adds 7,168 x 14,336 = 0.10B, for 11.6B by our count (the weights documentation lists 11.5B and does not show its arithmetic). Only 8 routed experts run per token, so the documentation lists just 2.4B **activated** parameters for the module, and that figure includes the shared embedding and head.

blocks.title: Where the MTP module's parameters sit (our count)

scenes.caption: Stored parameters: 256 routed experts dominate with 11.27B of the 11.6B. Attention is 0.19B, M_1 0.10B, the shared expert 0.04B and the router 0.002B.

blocks.md: Speculative decoding, the subject of lesson 7, speeds up generation: a cheap drafter guesses several tokens and the big model checks them all in one pass. EAGLE (Li et al., 2024) is one such method, and its drafter, like DeepSeek-V3's module, reads the big model's hidden state together with the embedding of the token one step ahead.

Parallel heads versus a sequential chain. In Gloeckle's design, head 3 must guess x(t+3) without knowing what x(t+1) and x(t+2) are. In DeepSeek-V3's design, depth k is told the true tokens up to t(i+k) during training, so each depth solves an ordinary one-step-further problem. The report notes the causal-chain idea resembles EAGLE but uses it to improve training.

blocks.question: At depth k = 2 in DeepSeek-V3's scheme, which inputs does the module use for position i, and which token does it predict?
options: h_i from the main model and Emb(t_i+1); predicts t_i+2
h_i from depth 1 and Emb(t_i+2); predicts t_i+3
h_i from depth 1 and Emb(t_i+3); predicts t_i+3
Only Emb(t_i+2); predicts t_i+3
blocks.explain: Depth k combines h at depth k - 1 with the embedding of t(i+k) and predicts t(i+k+1). For k = 2 that is h from depth 1, Emb(t(i+2)), and target t(i+3).

blocks.question: Why did the DeepSeek-V3 ablation conclude that MTP improved the model itself rather than just adding capacity?
options: The MTP models had more active parameters at inference
The module was discarded at inference, so the evaluated networks had identical cost and shape
MTP models were trained on more tokens
Only benchmarks that MTP helped were reported
blocks.explain: During evaluation the MTP module is dropped, so baseline and MTP models run the same main network at the same cost. The difference comes from how the shared weights were trained. The table even includes a regression (MMLU at large scale).

lessons.title: Add MTP to your GPT: both designs in about 60 lines

blocks.md: Time to write both designs into the GPT you built. Start with a tiny case: the 8-character chunk `Citizen:` from the Shakespeare text, positions 0 to 7. Head 1 at position 0 ('C') must predict 'i' at position 1; head 2 at the same position must predict 't' at position 2. Everything hinges on one slice: head $i$'s logits at positions 0 to $T - 1 - i$ pair with the tokens at positions $i$ to $T - 1$. Shift by the wrong amount and the model still trains, without an error, on a different task.

blocks.title: Pairing logits with targets: logits[:, :-i] with x[:, i:]

scenes.caption: One training chunk, T = 8. Each position's logits come from the prefix ending there.
Head 1: logits[:, :-1] keeps positions 0 to 6 and x[:, 1:] supplies 'i t i z e n :'. 7 pairs, the ordinary next-token loss.
Head 2: logits[:, :-2] keeps positions 0 to 5 and x[:, 2:] supplies 't i z e n :'. Positions 6 and 7 have nothing two ahead, so they drop out: 6 pairs.
Head 4: logits[:, :-4] with x[:, 4:]: 4 pairs, 'z e n :'. Over heads 1 to 4 the chunk gives 7 + 6 + 5 + 4 = 22 loss terms.
The silent bug: head 2 paired with x[:, 1:-1]. Shapes match (6 and 6), so nothing crashes, but head 2 learns the next token again and MTP does nothing.

blocks.code:
# ---- Design 1: Gloeckle et al., shared trunk + n parallel head blocks ----
class MTPGPT(nn.Module):
    def __init__(s, V, Tmax, d=128, nh=4, L=6, n=1):
        super().__init__()
        s.n = n
        s.wte, s.wpe = nn.Embedding(V, d), nn.Embedding(Tmax, d)
        s.trunk = nn.ModuleList(Block(d, nh) for _ in range(L - n))  # pay for heads
        s.heads = nn.ModuleList(Block(d, nh) for _ in range(n))       # head i = 1 block
        s.ln_f = nn.ModuleList(nn.LayerNorm(d) for _ in range(n))     # one per head
        s.lm_head = nn.Linear(d, V, bias=False)                        # shared f_u
        s.lm_head.weight = s.wte.weight                                # tied, as in GPT-2
        s.apply(init)

    def trunk_fwd(s, x):                       # x: [B, T] token ids
        z = s.wte(x) + s.wpe(torch.arange(x.size(1), device=x.device))
        for b in s.trunk:
            z = b(z)
        return z                               # [B, T, d]

    def head_logits(s, z, i):                  # head i predicts token t+i
        return s.lm_head(s.ln_f[i - 1](s.heads[i - 1](z)))  # [B, T, V]
blocks.caption: Gloeckle-style model. Block is the pre-LN transformer block you built; init applies a nanoGPT-style normal(0, 0.02) initialization (without nanoGPT's extra scaling of residual projections). With n heads the trunk has L - n blocks, so every n has L blocks in all.

blocks.md: Three wiring choices matter. The trunk loses one block for every head added, so the parameter count stays equal, as in the paper's comparisons. All heads call the same `lm_head`, which is also tied to the token embedding as in GPT-2, so the $d \times V$ matrix exists once. Each head gets its own final LayerNorm; the paper fixes only that the unembedding is shared, so that part is our choice (it adds $2d$ = 256 parameters per extra head at $d$ = 128). The loss and the memory-saving backward order from lesson 2 are a few lines more:

blocks.code:
def head_loss(logits, x, i):                   # position t is graded on x[t+i]
    return F.cross_entropy(logits[:, :-i].flatten(0, 1), x[:, i:].flatten())

def mtp_backward(model, x):                    # lesson 2's memory schedule
    z = model.trunk_fwd(x)
    z_leaf = z.detach().requires_grad_()
    losses = []
    for i in range(1, model.n + 1):
        loss_i = head_loss(model.head_logits(z_leaf, i), x, i)
        loss_i.backward()                      # grads add up in z_leaf.grad
        losses.append(loss_i.item())
    z.backward(z_leaf.grad)                    # one backward through the trunk
    return losses                              # [L_1, ..., L_n]; L_1 is next-token
blocks.caption: head_loss does the shift. mtp_backward is lesson 2's schedule: one head's logits alive at a time, gradients summed at the trunk output. The total loss is the plain sum of head losses, as in the paper.

blocks.md: Now DeepSeek-V3's depth-1 module, added to a plain $n = 1$ model. It follows equations 21 to 23 from lesson 4: RMSNorm the main model's final hidden state $h_i$ and the embedding of the true next token $t_{i+1}$, concatenate them, project $2d$ back to $d$ with $M_1$, run one block, and reuse the shared output head. Our hidden state is the last block's output before the final norm; the module's output goes through the same final norm and head as the main model.

blocks.code:
# ---- Design 2: DeepSeek-V3 style depth-1 module on a plain GPT (n = 1) ----
class MTPModule(nn.Module):
    def __init__(s, d, nh):
        super().__init__()
        s.norm_h, s.norm_e = nn.RMSNorm(d), nn.RMSNorm(d)
        s.M = nn.Linear(2 * d, d, bias=False)  # M_1: d x 2d
        s.block = Block(d, nh)                 # TRM_1
        s.apply(init)
    def forward(s, h, e):                      # h: [B, T-1, d], e: [B, T-1, d]
        return s.block(s.M(torch.cat([s.norm_h(h), s.norm_e(e)], dim=-1)))

def deepseek_loss(model, mtp, x, lam):         # model: MTPGPT with n = 1
    h = model.heads[0](model.trunk_fwd(x))     # main final hidden, [B, T, d]
    out = lambda u: model.lm_head(model.ln_f[0](u))   # shared output head
    L_main = head_loss(out(h), x, 1)           # predict t(i+1)
    h1 = mtp(h[:, :-1], model.wte(x[:, 1:]))   # h_i with Emb(t(i+1)): [B, T-1, d]
    L_mtp = F.cross_entropy(out(h1)[:, :-1].flatten(0, 1), x[:, 2:].flatten())
    return L_main + lam * L_mtp, L_main, L_mtp # predict t(i+2)
blocks.caption: DeepSeek-style module and loss. The embedding (wte) and the output head are the main model's own; only norm_h, norm_e, M and block are new. Total loss is L_main + lambda L_mtp, with D = 1 so no averaging over depths.

blocks.title: deepseek_loss on one batch: B = 2, T = 8, d = 32, V = 65
blocks.code:
def deepseek_loss(model, mtp, x, lam):         # model: MTPGPT with n = 1
    h = model.heads[0](model.trunk_fwd(x))     # main final hidden, [B, T, d]
    out = lambda u: model.lm_head(model.ln_f[0](u))   # shared output head
    L_main = head_loss(out(h), x, 1)           # predict t(i+1)
    h1 = mtp(h[:, :-1], model.wte(x[:, 1:]))   # h_i with Emb(t(i+1)): [B, T-1, d]
    L_mtp = F.cross_entropy(out(h1)[:, :-1].flatten(0, 1), x[:, 2:].flatten())
    return L_main + lam * L_mtp, L_main, L_mtp # predict t(i+2)

scenes.caption: The main model runs as usual and returns the last block's output for all 8 positions.
Main loss: logits at positions 0 to 6 against tokens 1 to 7, 7 targets per sequence.
Module input: h at positions 0 to 6 next to the embedding of tokens 1 to 7, the true next token at each position. Concatenated that is [2, 7, 64] before M projects it to 32.
MTP loss: module outputs at positions 0 to 5 against tokens 2 to 7. The last module output has no token two ahead, so 6 targets.
Weighted sum. With lam = 0 the result is exactly L_main, which the unit test checks bit for bit.

blocks.code:
# excerpt of test_mtp.py (B = 2, T = 8, d = 32, V = 65, L = 6)
m1 = MTPGPT(V, T, d=32, nh=4, L=6, n=1)
plain = list(m1.trunk) + list(m1.heads)          # the same 6 blocks in order
h = m1.wte(x) + m1.wpe(torch.arange(T))
for b in plain:
    h = b(h)
ref = F.cross_entropy(m1.lm_head(m1.ln_f[0](h))[:, :-1].flatten(0, 1), x[:, 1:].flatten())
mine = head_loss(m1.head_logits(m1.trunk_fwd(x), 1), x, 1)
assert torch.equal(ref, mine)
total, L_main, L_mtp = deepseek_loss(m1, mtp, x, lam=0.0)
assert torch.equal(total, L_main)

# output
# head 1: logits (2, 8, 65) used (2, 7, 65) targets (2, 7)
# head 2: logits (2, 8, 65) used (2, 6, 65) targets (2, 6)
# head 3: logits (2, 8, 65) used (2, 5, 65) targets (2, 5)
# head 4: logits (2, 8, 65) used (2, 4, 65) targets (2, 4)
# n=1 loss 4.144556045532227 4.144556045532227 equal: True

# lambda=0 total 4.144556045532227 main 4.144556045532227 equal: True

blocks.md: A small experiment, run on an Apple-silicon laptop. Data: the 1.1M-character tiny Shakespeare text with its 65 distinct characters, first 90% for training. Model: $d$ = 128, 4 attention heads, 6 blocks in total, context 128, batch 32, AdamW at a peak learning rate of 1e-3 with warmup and cosine decay, 5,000 steps, 2 seeds. Gloeckle runs with $n$ = 1, 2 and 4 have equal size (1,214,592 parameters, plus 256 per extra head norm). The DeepSeek-style run adds a depth-1 module with $\lambda$ = 0.3, 231,296 extra parameters, so it is **not** size-matched. Every run is scored on the same 40 validation batches with the **next-token head only**, the head you would decode with.

blocks.prompt: Lesson 3 showed MTP losing to next-token training for the smallest code models (0.3B and 0.6B parameters). Our models have 1.2M parameters and predict single characters. What do you expect for the next-token validation loss of n = 2 and n = 4 against n = 1?
blocks.reveal: Mixed, and smaller than you might think. Averaged over 2 seeds, n = 1 reached 1.506 nats, n = 2 reached 1.499 (slightly lower in both seeds) and n = 4 reached 1.5425, clearly worse. The n = 2 gain of 0.007 is smaller than the 0.011 gap between the two n = 1 seeds, so treat it as a tie. The n = 4 loss is not noise: both seeds sit well outside the n = 1 spread. A likely cause is depth: its trunk keeps only 2 of the 6 blocks, so the next-token path is 3 blocks deep instead of 6.

Mean of 2 seeds: n = 1 1.506, n = 2 1.499, n = 4 1.5425, DeepSeek-style 1.496. Bars from zero look alike on purpose: every difference is under 0.05 nats.

blocks.md: Read this as a wiring check, not evidence about MTP. It is 2 seeds at 1.2M parameters, far below the scales where Gloeckle et al. saw gains, and the DeepSeek-style run's 0.010 edge over n = 1 is about the size of the 0.011 gap between the two n = 1 seeds and comes with 19% more parameters during training. What the run does show: the code trains, the next-token head stays usable, and taking parameters from the trunk (n = 4) costs quality at this size.

blocks.question: A colleague's MTP model trains fine, but its head-2 loss tracks the head-1 loss almost exactly from the first step. They compute head 2's loss as cross_entropy(logits2[:, :-2], x[:, 1:-1]). What is wrong?
options: Nothing; head 2 is expected to match head 1
logits2 should be sliced [:, 2:] instead of [:, :-2]
cross_entropy needs the targets one-hot encoded
The targets are shifted by 1 instead of 2, so head 2 is learning the next token again
blocks.explain: Position t must be paired with x[t+2]: logits2[:, :-2] with x[:, 2:]. With x[:, 1:-1] the shapes still match, so nothing crashes, but every pair is (position t, token t+1), the next-token task. Slicing the logits [:, 2:] would pair later positions with earlier tokens.

blocks.question: Your Gloeckle-style model uses n = 4 heads with L = 6 blocks in total. How many trunk blocks does it have, and why does that matter for comparing against n = 1?
options: 2 trunk blocks plus 4 head blocks, so all models have 6 blocks and gains cannot come from extra parameters
6 trunk blocks plus 4 heads; MTP models are meant to be larger
5 trunk blocks, as for n = 1, so only the heads differ
0 trunk blocks; heads replace the trunk
blocks.explain: The trunk has L - n = 2 blocks. Adding head blocks while removing trunk blocks keeps the total at 6, matching the paper's equal-parameter comparisons. It also means a 4-head model has a much shallower shared trunk, one reason MTP can hurt small models.

lessons.title: The design space: ProphetNet to registers, and MTP in open models

blocks.md: You have now seen two ways to ask a position about the future: Gloeckle's parallel heads and DeepSeek-V3's chained modules. They are points in a larger design space, and the choice decides what each extra prediction sees, what it costs, and whether it can draft tokens later. Keep one tiny question in mind for every design: with the prefix 'the cat sat', how does the model get asked for 'the', two tokens ahead, and is anything left over at inference time?

**ProphetNet (Qi et al., Microsoft, 2020)** came first. It is an encoder-decoder model (the encoder reads a source text, the decoder writes the output) pretrained on **future n-gram prediction**: at each step the decoder predicts the next $n$ tokens at once, with $n = 2$ in pretraining. An n-gram is a run of $n$ consecutive tokens. Its **n-stream self-attention** adds $n$ predicting streams beside the ordinary main stream; the $i$-th stream starts from a special token instead of the previous token and attends to the main stream's hidden states to predict the token $i$ steps ahead. The streams share all their weights with the main stream, so they add no layers and can simply be switched off for fine-tuning or inference. The stated motivation is the same as Gloeckle's: stop the model overfitting to strong local correlations.

**MuToR (Gerontopoulos et al., 2025, 'Multi-Token Prediction Needs Registers')** removes the extra heads entirely. It interleaves **register tokens** into the training sequence: special tokens that share one learnable embedding and are never shown at inference. A register placed after $x_t$ is trained to predict $x_{t+d}$, with the offset $d$ sampled per sequence from 1 to $d_{max}$. Two masking rules make the registers invisible to the main task: regular tokens cannot attend to any register, and registers cannot attend to each other. The offset is encoded only through the register's position id, $t + d - 1$, the position of the regular token that would normally predict $x_{t+d}$. The figure shows the mask for $d = 2$.

blocks.title: MuToR attention mask, 4 tokens with registers, d = 2

scenes.caption: Rows are queries, columns are keys; 1 means the row may attend to the column. The sequence is x1, r, x2, r, x3, r, x4, and each register is labeled with its target two tokens ahead.

Regular tokens (rows x1 to x4) see only earlier regular tokens, exactly the causal mask of the plain model. Their predictions cannot depend on registers, which is why registers can be dropped at inference.
Each register sees the regular tokens up to its position and itself, never another register. The register after x2 predicts x4 from x1, x2 and its own embedding.
Masked pairs (0) are the rule at work: register columns are blocked for every other row. The register after x3 would predict x5, which lies past this sequence, so it gets no loss term.

blocks.md: Because MuToR adds only one embedding vector and no layers, it suits **fine-tuning** an existing model. Its loss is $(1 - a)\mathcal{L}_{ntp} + a\,\mathcal{L}_{reg}$, a weighted mix of the next-token and register losses. Fine-tuning Gemma 2B (a 2-billion-parameter open model from Google) on the GSM8K grade-school math training split, the paper reports 38.87% accuracy for next-token fine-tuning, 40.66% for Gloeckle-style heads adapted to fine-tuning and 42.10% for MuToR. The price is compute: interleaving registers lengthens every training sequence. The authors trained the baselines for more epochs, roughly doubling their compute, and report that this did not close the gap.

**Why not just bolt heads onto a trained model?** Mehra et al. (Sony, 2025) tested it on Pythia models (EleutherAI's open suite of research models; here 410M to 2.8B parameters) by giving each head the structure of the final transformer layer (the next-token head starts as a copy of it, the head for the token two ahead from random weights) and training the heads on a translation task with the backbone frozen. They project each intermediate layer's output through the unembedding and measure how close it already is to the final next-token distribution (a KL divergence): in large models it gets close well before the last layer. Their reading is that the hidden layers **specialize for next-token prediction** and discard information a two-ahead head would need. Training the backbone jointly with the heads helps but does not close the gap to a baseline that computes the second token exactly by summing over every possible first token, which is accurate but costly: a sum over the whole vocabulary for each extra token.

blocks.title: Second-token top-5 accuracy, Pythia 2.8B (Mehra et al., Table 1)

scenes.caption: Baseline: marginalizing over the first token with the fine-tuned model itself gets the true second token into its top 5 77.7% of the time.
A head trained on a frozen next-token backbone: 60.7%. The backbone's features were not built for the token two ahead.
Fine-tuning the backbone too (with LoRA adapters) raises it to 64.5%, and a higher learning rate for the heads to 66.7%. Better, still well short of 77.7%.

blocks.md:
This agrees with lesson 3, where adding a 4-token loss to an already trained Llama 2 brought no significant gain, and it is the background for Medusa in lesson 7, whose heads are trained after the fact for drafting only. Heads learned jointly from the start of pretraining are the strong version.

**Adoption.** The sequential module has become a common part of open releases. DeepSeek-V3 ships one MTP module. Xiaomi's MiMo-7B trains a single MTP layer in pretraining, because more layers gave no further gain in its preliminary studies, with loss weight 0.3 for the first 10.3T tokens and then 0.1; for inference it adds more MTP layers, trained afterwards with the main model and first layer frozen. GLM-4.5 (Z.ai) sets `num_nextn_predict_layers` to 1 in its `config.json`, and the model card of Qwen3-Next (the Qwen team's 80B-parameter mixture-of-experts model with 3B active per token) lists MTP both for pretraining quality and for faster inference.

The four designs side by side:

```
design       depth k sees          extra params        drafter?
ProphetNet   prefix (own stream)   none, shared        no, streams off
Gloeckle     prefix only           n-1 head layers *   yes, one pass
DeepSeek-V3  prefix + true tokens  block + d x 2d      yes, 1 per module
             up to t+k             per depth           (chainable)
MuToR        prefix + register     one embedding       no, registers off
```

(* paid for by removing as many trunk layers.) Training cost grows differently: Gloeckle adds one head layer plus one unembedding per extra token, DeepSeek-V3 one block plus one unembedding per depth, MuToR a longer input sequence, and ProphetNet extra streams through every decoder layer.

Every MTP design asks a position about tokens further ahead; they differ in what that prediction may see (prefix only, or true tokens in between), where the parameters live (none, heads, a module, one embedding), and whether anything is kept for drafting. Joint training from pretraining beats bolting heads on later.

blocks.question: A team wants the MTP training signal while fine-tuning an existing 8B chat model, with no change to the deployed architecture and almost no new parameters. Which design fits best?
options: Gloeckle-style parallel heads, keeping the parameter count by removing trunk layers
A DeepSeek-V3-style module with its own MoE block
MuToR register tokens, dropped at inference
ProphetNet, since its streams share weights
blocks.explain: MuToR adds one register embedding, needs no new layers, and its mask keeps regular tokens blind to registers, so the deployed model is unchanged. Removing trunk layers would break a pretrained model, a DeepSeek module adds a block, and ProphetNet's n-stream attention is an encoder-decoder pretraining design.

blocks.question: Mehra et al. trained a second-token head on a frozen Pythia backbone and got 60.7% top-5 accuracy against 77.7% for exact marginalization. What is their explanation?
options: The head had too few parameters to learn the task
Top-5 accuracy is the wrong metric for the second token
The unembedding was not shared between heads
The backbone's later layers specialize for next-token prediction and discard what a two-ahead head needs
blocks.explain: Projecting intermediate layers through the unembedding shows them already close to the final next-token distribution in large models, so information useful for the second token is gone by the time the head reads it. Joint training recovers part of the gap (66.7% at best), not all.

lessons.title: Reusing the extra heads to decode faster

blocks.md: Decoding a large model is usually memory-bandwidth bound: each step reads all the weights to produce one token. Fetching a weight from GPU memory takes far longer than the one multiply and add done with it for that token, so the step's time is set by how fast memory delivers bytes (its bandwidth), not by arithmetic. **Speculative decoding** (Leviathan et al., 2023) uses a cheap draft to propose several tokens and the big model to check them all in one forward pass. MTP models carry their own drafter, the extra heads, so they can do this **without a separate draft model**. Gloeckle et al. use blockwise parallel decoding (Stern, Shazeer and Uszkoreit, 2018), which is greedy self-speculation: the model drafts for itself and verifies with greedy decoding, always taking the most likely token.

The greedy rule is simple. The $n$ heads propose the next $n$ tokens, one each. Head 1's proposal is the main model's own greedy token, so it is always correct. The next forward pass runs the model on the drafted tokens; at each drafted position the next-token head says what it would have produced. Keep the drafts up to the first disagreement. Because the check uses the next-token head itself, the output is **identical** to ordinary greedy decoding with that head; only the number of forward passes changes.

blocks.title: One draft-and-verify cycle with 4 heads

scenes.caption: Context 'for i in'. One forward pass runs all four heads at the last position. (Illustrative tokens.)
The heads propose 'range', '(', 'n', ')'. Head 1's token 'range' is the true greedy token; the other three are guesses.
Next forward pass over the drafts. After 'range', head 1 says '(' (match). After '(', it says 'len', not 'n' (mismatch). Later drafts are discarded.
Emitted: 'range', '(' and head 1's correction 'len'. In that same pass, heads 2 to 4 at the '(' position already drafted the tokens after 'len', so the next cycle needs no extra pass.

blocks.md: How many tokens does each forward pass yield on average? A simplified model: suppose each draft after the first is accepted with probability $a$, independently, given that the previous ones were. With $k$ extra drafts the expected tokens per forward is a geometric sum. Draft $j$ counts only if it and every draft before it are accepted, which has probability $a^j$, so the expected count is 1 plus $a$ plus $a^2$ up to $a^k$, and the geometric series formula sums that to $(1 - a^{k+1})/(1 - a)$.

blocks.tex: \mathbb{E}[\text{tokens per forward}] = 1 + a + a^2 + \dots + a^{k} = \frac{1 - a^{k+1}}{1 - a}
blocks.caption: Simplified: real acceptance rates differ by head and by context, and drafts are not independent. The first term 1 is the token the main head always contributes.

blocks.title: Expected tokens per forward pass vs acceptance rate

scenes.caption: One extra draft (DeepSeek-V3 with D = 1). Its report gives an 85% to 90% acceptance rate for the second token, which this model turns into 1.85 to 1.90 tokens per forward.
Two extra drafts: at a = 0.85 the model gives 2.57 tokens per forward. Each extra draft adds less, because it only counts if all earlier ones were accepted.
Three extra drafts (four heads): 3.19 at a = 0.85 and 3.44 at a = 0.9. The ceiling is 1 + k, reached only if every draft is accepted.

blocks.md: Measured numbers. Gloeckle et al. ran greedy self-speculative decoding on their 7B 4-token code model (prompts and 512-token completions from unseen test data, batch size 42). Using 2, 3 and 4 heads gave 1.94, 2.78 and 3.50 tokens per forward and relative speedups of 1.85x, 2.54x and 3.05x. For an 8-byte prediction byte-level model the speedup reached 6.4x. DeepSeek-V3 reports 1.8 times the tokens per second with its single MTP module.

DeepSeek-V3's 1.8x comes from a single module drafting a single token. Can one depth-1 module draft more? Serving engines do it by **chaining** the module: feed it its own output. Step 1 combines the main model's hidden state with the embedding of the token just produced and drafts one token. Step 2 runs the **same** module again on its own step-1 output hidden state and the embedding of its own draft, and drafts the next. In the DeepSeek MTP code of vLLM (a widely used open-source LLM serving engine) the layer for draft step $s$ is chosen as $s$ modulo the number of MTP layers, so with one layer every step reuses layer 61, and a comment notes that each step's hidden state is recycled into the next.

blocks.title: Chaining one MTP module to draft two tokens

scenes.caption: The main model's pass emits token t+1 from its own head and exposes its final hidden state h_t.
Step 1 is exactly what the module was trained on: the main model's h_t plus the embedding of the real token t+1. It drafts t+2.
Step 2 reuses the same weights, but its inputs are its own step-1 hidden state and the embedding of its own draft. Training never showed it its own hidden state, and the draft token may be wrong.
The next main-model pass verifies t+2 and t+3 together. The second draft counts only if the first was accepted, and it is accepted less often.

blocks.md:
Expect each extra chained step to be accepted less often. The module was trained only at depth 1, with the main model's hidden state and a true token as inputs; at step 2 both inputs are its own guesses. MiMo-7B (Xiaomi, 2025) shows the effect from the other side: rather than chain one layer, it trained extra MTP layers for later steps, and reports about 90% acceptance for the first layer and still above 75% for the third. The vLLM MTP docs call `num_speculative_tokens` the speculative depth and recommend starting with 1.

So replace the single rate $a$ with **per-position** rates: $a_1$ for the first draft, $a_2$ for the second given that the first was accepted. With $a_1 = 0.85$ and $a_2 = 0.6$:

blocks.caption: Draft 2 counts only if both drafts are accepted, probability a1 a2 = 0.51. With one rate a = 0.85 for both steps the same formula gives 1 + 0.85 + 0.7225 = 2.57, too optimistic for a chained depth-1 module.

blocks.title: Tokens per forward: one draft versus two chained drafts

scenes.caption: One draft at 85% acceptance: 1.85 tokens per forward, the low end of DeepSeek-V3's reported range.
If the second draft were as good as the first, a second step would add 0.85 x 0.85 = 0.72 tokens: 2.57.
With the second step at 60% conditional acceptance it adds only 0.51: 2.36. The extra step also costs a module pass, so measure before raising the depth.

blocks.code:
# Qwen3-Next model card: vLLM with its MTP layer drafting 2 tokens per step
vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct --port 8000 \
  --tensor-parallel-size 4 --max-model-len 262144 \
  --speculative-config '{"method":"qwen3_next_mtp","num_speculative_tokens":2}'

# vLLM MTP docs: a model with native MTP layers, depth 1
vllm serve XiaomiMiMo/MiMo-7B-Base --tensor-parallel-size 1 \
  --speculative-config '{"method":"mtp","num_speculative_tokens":1}'
blocks.caption: Commands as given on the Qwen3-Next model card and in the vLLM MTP docs (not run here: they need multi-GPU servers). Check the current docs for method names, which change between releases.

blocks.title: Tokens per forward vs real speedup (Gloeckle Table S2, code)

scenes.caption: Tokens produced per forward pass. 3.50 with all four heads, out of a maximum of 4.

Wall-clock speedup is lower: 1.85x, 2.54x, 3.05x. A verifying pass processes several positions and runs extra heads, so it costs a bit more than a plain decode step (speedup over tokens per forward: 0.95, 0.91, 0.87).

blocks.prompt: Pretrained 4-token heads versus heads bolted on afterwards: which should draft better?
blocks.reveal: Pretrained heads. Gloeckle et al. note that pretraining with the multi-token loss makes the extra heads much more accurate than simply finetuning a next-token model, which unlocks the full speedup. **Medusa** (Cai et al., 2024) is the bolt-on approach: extra decoding heads trained on top of a frozen model (Medusa-1, over 2.2x) or jointly with it (Medusa-2, 2.3x to 3.6x), drafting several candidates per head and verifying them with tree attention: the candidates form a tree of possible continuations, and an attention mask lets one forward pass check every branch.

blocks.md: Lossless means 'same output as greedy decoding with the next-token head'. With temperature sampling, comparing argmax tokens would change the output distribution. The speculative sampling rule of Leviathan et al. keeps it exact: accept a drafted token x with probability min(1, p(x)/q(x)), where p is the big model's probability and q the drafter's, and on rejection resample from max(0, p - q), renormalized. Leviathan et al. prove it in general; here is a two-token check.

blocks.title: Speculative sampling on two tokens: p = (0.6, 0.4), q = (0.9, 0.1)

scenes.caption: The verifier wants p(A) = 0.6, p(B) = 0.4. The drafter over-proposes A: q(A) = 0.9, q(B) = 0.1.
Accept A with min(1, 0.6/0.9) = 2/3, so A is proposed and kept with probability 0.9 x 2/3 = 0.6. B is always kept: 0.1. Total acceptance 0.7.

Rejection has probability 0.3. The residual max(0, p - q) = (0, 0.3) normalizes to (0, 1), so every rejection becomes B: 0.1 + 0.3 = 0.4. Output equals p exactly; 200,000 simulated draws gave 0.597 and 0.403.

blocks.md:
**Tradeoffs to keep in mind.**

- Training: extra head layers or modules cost compute and memory (DeepSeek-V3's module alone has 11.5B unique parameters), and the per-head memory schedule is needed to avoid the nV logit blow-up.
- Quality: gains depend on scale and data; small models, multiple-choice benchmarks and some natural-language settings show no gain or regressions, and $n$ needs tuning.
- Inference: drafting pays off when decoding is memory-bound. If a server is already compute-bound at large batch (many batched requests share each weight read, so arithmetic becomes the limit), extra verification work can eat the gain, so measure on your workload.

MTP gives two separate benefits: a training signal that can make the main model better, and heads that can draft tokens for exact, faster greedy decoding. You can use the first without the second by discarding the heads.

blocks.question: A model with one MTP layer is served with num_speculative_tokens = 3, so the layer is chained three times. Measured conditional acceptance is 0.9, 0.6 and 0.4 for the three drafts. Expected tokens per forward, under the simplified model?
options: 4.0, because three drafts plus the main token
3.44, as if all three steps were accepted at 0.9
1.9, because chained drafts are never accepted
blocks.explain: Draft j counts only if drafts 1 to j are all accepted: 0.9, then 0.9 x 0.6 = 0.54, then 0.54 x 0.4 = 0.216. Adding the main token gives 2.656. Using one rate of 0.9 for all three would give 3.44 and overstate the gain.

blocks.question: An MTP model with one extra draft has acceptance rate 0.9. Under the simplified independence model, about how many tokens does each forward pass yield, and why is the measured speedup lower?
options: 1.9 tokens; verification passes cost a little more than plain decode steps
2.0 tokens; the draft is always accepted at greedy temperature
1.81 tokens, because 0.9 squared is 0.81
1.9 tokens; the speedup is lower because outputs differ from greedy decoding
blocks.explain: Expected tokens = 1 + a = 1.9. The wall-clock gain is smaller because each verifying pass processes extra positions and runs the drafter. Output does not differ: greedy verification reproduces greedy decoding exactly. DeepSeek-V3 reports 85% to 90% acceptance and 1.8x tokens per second.

blocks.question: You serve a Gloeckle-style 4-token model with greedy decoding and enable self-speculative decoding with all 4 heads. What happens to the generated text?
options: It becomes more diverse because heads 2 to 4 inject their own choices
It is identical to greedy decoding with head 1; only the number of forward passes drops
It is identical only if every draft is accepted
It degrades slightly, which is the price of a 3x speedup
blocks.explain: Every emitted token is one that head 1 would have chosen given the same prefix: drafts are kept only when they match head 1's prediction, and the first mismatch is replaced by head 1's token. Acceptance rate changes speed, never content.
